kernels.definition: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.

definitionAnchor.quote: The outermost chemical layer and the one we currently reside on is the crust

facts.text: The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.

anchor.quote: The mantle sits below the crust and above the core

facts.text: The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.

anchor.quote: The core of the Earth has both liquid and solid layers and consists mostly of iron, nickel, and possibly some oxygen

facts.text: The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.

anchor.quote: this layer moves and flows due to convection currents created by heat coming from the earth's core

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

kernels.definition: Plate tectonics holds that Earth's rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the ductile asthenosphere; most geologic action occurs at their three kinds of boundaries.

definitionAnchor.quote: Plate boundaries are where most of Earth's geologic action occurs

facts.text: At divergent boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created.

anchor.quote: At divergent boundaries, sometimes called constructive boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other

facts.text: At convergent boundaries, two or more plates move toward each other and lithosphere is destroyed.

anchor.quote: Convergent boundaries, also called destructive boundaries, are places where two or more plates move toward each other

facts.text: At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past each other.

anchor.quote: A transform boundary is where the lithospheric plates slide past each other in the horizontal plane

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.4 Plate boundaries

kernels.definition: An earthquake releases stored elastic energy when rock slips along a fault; the energy travels outward as seismic waves, including fast compressional P waves and slower shear S waves.

definitionAnchor.quote: Earthquakes are felt at the surface of the Earth when energy is released by blocks of rock sliding past each other, i.e. faulting has occurred

facts.text: Elastic rebound theory explains earthquakes: stored energy is released and the broken rock springs back toward its original position.

anchor.quote: The release of seismic energy is explained by the elastic rebound theory

facts.text: P waves are the fastest body waves and move by compression, like sound through air, so they travel through solids, liquids, and gases.

anchor.quote: enabling them to travel through solids, liquids, plasma, and gases

facts.text: S waves are slower shear waves restricted to lateral motion, so they travel only through solids, never liquids.

anchor.quote: S waves can only travel through solids but not liquids, plasma, or gases

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §9.1 Earthquakes and seismic waves

mcItems.q: Which layer of Earth is described as solid rock that flows slowly due to convection?
mcItems.ex: The asthenosphere is the correct choice because it is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat (Claim 3). The most plausible misconception is selecting the rocky mantle, which is described as thick and solid rock, not flowing.

mcItems.q: What material primarily composes the core layers?
mcItems.ex: Iron and nickel is the correct answer because the core is made mostly of these materials (Claim 2). The most plausible misconception is selecting silicates, which are characteristic of the crust and mantle, not the core.

mcItems.q: Which boundary type is characterized by plates sliding horizontally past one another?
mcItems.ex: The correct choice, Transform boundary, describes plates sliding horizontally past each other. A common misconception is confusing this with a divergent boundary, which involves plates moving away from each other.

mcItems.q: Where is new lithosphere generated as lithospheric plates move apart?
mcItems.ex: The correct choice, Divergent boundary, is where new lithosphere is created as plates move away from each other. A plausible misconception is selecting a convergent boundary, which involves lithosphere destruction.
